results.parsed_rule: When an appeal under this section is laid before another Judge of that Court, and that Judge so requires, the appeal shall be re-heard and decided by a larger Bench of Judges.
results.parsed_conclusion: The third tie-breaking judge does not have to conduct a completely new trial with all the witnesses.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule addresses re-hearing of appeals by a larger bench of judges, not the conduct of a completely new trial with witnesses, so the Conclusion's statement that a new trial is not required is consistent with the Rule's framework of appellate re-hearing.

results.parsed_rule: In order to corroborate the testimony of a witness, any former statement made by such witness relating to the same fact, at or about the time when the fact took place, or before any authority legally competent to investigate the fact, may be proved.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, a witness cannot use a diary entry they wrote five years after the event to corroborate their current testimony.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule requires the former statement to be made "at or about the time when the fact took place" or before a legally competent authority, and a diary entry written five years after the event fails to meet either of these temporal requirements for corroboration.

results.parsed_rule: "On examining any record under section 438 or otherwise, the High Court or the Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate by himself or by any of the Magistrates subordinate to him to make, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate may himself make or direct any subordinate Magistrate to make, further inquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 226 or sub-section (4) of section 227, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharged: Provided that no Court shall make any direction under this section for inquiry into the case of any person who has been discharged unless such person has had an opportunity of showing cause why such direction should not be made."
results.parsed_conclusion: Section 439 does not give the Sessions Judge the power to directly *convict* a person who was previously discharged.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule only authorizes the Sessions Judge to direct further inquiry into cases of discharged persons, but contains no provision granting power to directly convict anyone.

results.parsed_rule: Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly, or with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or to any person, cancels, destroys or defaces, or attempts to cancel, destroy or deface, or secretes or attempts to secrete any document which is or purports to be a will, or an authority to adopt a son, or any valuable security, or commits mischief in respect of such document, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, the person is not guilty under Section 343.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule describes offenses related to fraudulently canceling, destroying, defacing, or secreting documents like wills or valuable securities, but makes no mention of "Section 343" or any circumstances under which a person would not be guilty of such offenses.

results.parsed_rule: "When an Executive Magistrate receives information that there is within his local jurisdiction a person taking precautions to conceal his presence and that there is reason to believe that he is doing so with a view to committing a cognizable offence, the Magistrate may, in the manner hereinafter provided, require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond for his good behaviour for such period, not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit."
results.parsed_conclusion: The authority to require a suspected person to show cause under Section 128 of BNSS 2023 lies with the Executive Magistrate.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that "the Magistrate may... require such person to show cause," and the opening clause specifies this power belongs to an "Executive Magistrate" who receives the relevant information within his local jurisdiction.

results.parsed_rule: Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, the defense does not apply to euthanasia where a doctor intentionally gives a lethal injection to a consenting patient to end their suffering.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states it applies to acts "not intended to cause death," whereas euthanasia by lethal injection is specifically intended to cause death, so the Conclusion correctly identifies that the defense does not apply, but this is directly supported by (not contradicted by or unaddressed in) the Rule's plain text.

results.parsed_rule:
"In every case in which a commission is issued under section 319,
the inquiry, trial or other proceeding may be adjourned for a specified time reasonably sufficient for the
execution and return of the commission."
results.parsed_conclusion: No, the judge is not *forced* to adjourn the entire trial just because one witness is being examined by commission; they may adjourn only the relevant portion.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule states the proceeding "may be adjourned" (not "must be" or "shall be"), which supports the Conclusion's assertion that the judge is not forced to adjourn, and the Rule's allowance for adjournment of "the inquiry, trial or other proceeding" is consistent with the Conclusion's interpretation that only the relevant portion need be adjourned rather than the entire trial.

results.parsed_rule: The High Court may, whenever it appears to it to be expedient or necessary, confer the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or of the second class on any member of the Judicial Service of the State, functioning as a Judge in a Civil Court.
results.parsed_conclusion: Yes, it is possible for a Civil Court Judge to exercise the powers of a Criminal Magistrate if granted such authority by the High Court.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that the High Court may confer the powers of a Judicial Magistrate (a criminal court position) on a member of the Judicial Service functioning as a Judge in a Civil Court, which directly supports the Conclusion's claim that a Civil Court Judge can exercise Criminal Magistrate powers if granted by the High Court.

results.parsed_rule: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both and in case of second or subsequent conviction of any person under this section, he shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years and with fine.
results.parsed_conclusion: Yes, the person has committed theft.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule prescribes punishments for theft but does not establish whether any particular person has actually committed theft; the Conclusion makes a factual determination about guilt that the Rule (a sentencing provision) does not address.

results.parsed_rule: "Police officers superior in rank to an officer in charge of a police station may exercise the same powers, throughout the local area to which they are appointed, as may be exercised by such officer within the limits of his station."
results.parsed_conclusion: A superior officer's power extends beyond just administrative tasks and encompasses all powers exercisable by an officer in charge of a police station within their local area.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that superior officers "may exercise the same powers" as an officer in charge of a police station throughout their local area, which directly supports the Conclusion's claim that superior officers' powers encompass all powers (not just administrative tasks) exercisable by station officers.

results.parsed_rule: "Whenever any person is convicted of an offence for which under this Sanhita the Court has power to sentence him to rigorous imprisonment, the Court may, by its sentence, order that the offender shall be kept in solitary confinement for any portion or portions of the imprisonment to which he is sentenced, not exceeding three months in the whole, according to the following scale, namely: — (a) a time not exceeding one month if the term of imprisonment shall not exceed six months; (b) a time not exceeding two months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed six months and shall not exceed one year; (c) a time not exceeding three months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed one year."
results.parsed_conclusion: The total duration of solitary confinement cannot exceed three months based on the total length of the sentence.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that solitary confinement cannot exceed "three months in the whole" and provides a scale that caps the maximum at three months for sentences exceeding one year, which directly supports the Conclusion's claim about the three-month maximum based on sentence length.

results.parsed_rule: The State Government may, either on its own motion or on the application of any person aggrieved, rescind or alter any order made by it under the proviso to sub-section (4).
results.parsed_conclusion: An emergency order under Section 163 can last longer than two months if directed by the State Government.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule addresses the State Government's power to rescind or alter orders made under a proviso to sub-section (4), but says nothing about emergency orders under Section 163 or their duration beyond two months.

results.parsed_rule: Nothing in this section, section 478 or section 480, shall be deemed to require the release of any person liable to be detained for some matter other than that in respect of which the bond or bail bond was executed.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, the jailor cannot wait until the next morning to process the release because his shift is ending.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule addresses whether certain sections require release of persons detained for matters unrelated to their bond, but says nothing about a jailor's shift timing or processing delays for release.

results.parsed_rule: If a document is required by law to be attested, it shall not be used as evidence until one attesting witness at least has been called for the purpose of proving its execution, if there be an attesting witness alive, and subject to the process of the Court and capable of giving evidence. Provided that it shall not be necessary to call an attesting witness in proof of the execution of any document, not being a will, which has been registered in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), unless its execution by the person by whom it purports to have been executed is specifically denied.
results.parsed_conclusion: It is not always necessary to call an attesting witness for a registered sale deed if no one denies who signed it.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly provides that calling an attesting witness is not necessary for registered documents (other than wills) unless execution is specifically denied, which directly supports the Conclusion's statement about registered sale deeds.

results.parsed_rule: (1) When a Court of Session or Court of a Magistrate of the first class convicts a person of any of the offences specified in sub-section (2) or of abetting any such offence and is of opinion that it is necessary to take security from such person for keeping the peace, the Court may, at the time of passing sentence on such person, order him to execute a bond or bail bond, for keeping the peace for such period, not exceeding three years, as it thinks fit.
results.parsed_conclusion: The maximum duration for which a court can order someone to keep the peace under this section is three years.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that the bond for keeping the peace can be ordered "for such period, not exceeding three years," which directly supports the Conclusion's claim that three years is the maximum duration.

results.parsed_rule: "Any Judicial Magistrate may recall any case made over by him under sub-section (2) of section 212 to any other Magistrate and may inquire into or try such cases himself."
results.parsed_conclusion: The retrieved text does not provide sufficient information to determine if a regular First Class Magistrate can withdraw a case from another First Class Magistrate who sits in the next courtroom over.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that "Any Judicial Magistrate may recall any case made over by him" which directly addresses whether a Magistrate can withdraw a case from another Magistrate (specifically, one they previously transferred), contradicting the Conclusion's claim that there is insufficient information to determine this.

results.parsed_rule: No appeal shall lie against the judgment under this section unless the proclaimed offender presents himself before the Court of appeal.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, a lawyer cannot immediately file an appeal to the High Court while the offender is still hiding abroad.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule requires the proclaimed offender to present himself before the Court of appeal as a prerequisite for any appeal, which directly supports the Conclusion that an appeal cannot be filed while the offender remains in hiding abroad.

results.parsed_rule: "A District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner of Police empowered by the State Government or the District Magistrate in this behalf, may order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance..."
results.parsed_conclusion: No, a random Executive Magistrate cannot issue a prohibition order under Section 162 of BNSS 2023.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that "any other Executive Magistrate" empowered by the State Government or District Magistrate may issue such orders, which directly contradicts the Conclusion's claim that "a random Executive Magistrate cannot issue a prohibition order."

results.parsed_rule: When any statement of which evidence is given forms part of a longer statement, or of a conversation or part of an isolated document, or is contained in a document which forms part of a book, or is contained in part of electronic record or of a connected series of letters or papers, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the statement, conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers as the Court considers necessary in that particular case to the full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement, and of the circumstances under which it was made.
results.parsed_conclusion: The statutory text does not provide a rigid rule on exactly how many sentences surrounding a statement must be included; rather, it allows for discretion based on the Court's judgment.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly grants the Court discretion to determine how much of the surrounding material should be admitted ("so much and no more... as the Court considers necessary"), which directly supports the Conclusion's claim that there is no rigid rule but rather court-based discretion.

results.parsed_rule: "Every summons issued by a Court under this Sanhita shall be,—in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer of such Court or by such other officer as the High Court may, from time to times, by rule direct..."
results.parsed_conclusion: A physical summons is not necessarily required to be signed specifically by the presiding officer of the Court.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly requires that every summons "shall be...signed by the presiding officer of such Court or by such other officer as the High Court may...direct," which directly contradicts the Conclusion's claim that a summons is "not necessarily required to be signed specifically by the presiding officer" - the Rule mandates signature by either the presiding officer OR another officer as directed by the High Court, meaning a specific authorized signature is always required.

results.parsed_rule: A confession is irrelevant if it appears to the Court that the making of the confession was caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person, proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient to give the accused person grounds which would appear reasonable for supposing he could gain an advantage or avoid an evil of a temporal nature.
results.parsed_conclusion: A confession is deemed irrelevant if caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise from authority sufficient to influence the accused.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion faithfully restates the core elements of the Rule—that a confession becomes irrelevant when caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise from a person in authority that is sufficient to influence the accused—even though it compresses the Rule's more detailed language about "reasonable grounds" for supposing advantage or avoiding evil.

results.parsed_rule: "A Sessions Judge or Magistrate making an order under section 448, section 449, section 450 or section 451 shall record his reasons for making it."
results.parsed_conclusion: Judges who fail to record their reasons for transferring criminal cases will be in violation of the law as stated.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule requires judges to record reasons when making orders under sections 448-451, but the Conclusion assumes those sections concern "transferring criminal cases," which is not stated or established anywhere in the Rule text provided.

results.parsed_rule: "Every police officer making an investigation under this Chapter shall day by day enter his proceedings in the investigation in a diary, setting forth the time at which the information reached him, the time at which he began and closed his investigation, the place or places visited by him, and a statement of the circumstances ascertained through his investigation."
results.parsed_conclusion: Police officers are required to keep a daily log of their investigation activities as per the rule provided in the statutory text.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates the Rule's requirement that police officers must make day-by-day entries of their investigation proceedings in a diary, which is faithfully captured by the phrase "daily log of their investigation activities."

results.parsed_rule: No such person shall in any case be detained during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial for more than the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the said offence under that law.
results.parsed_conclusion: A person cannot be held in jail for more than the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the offense during their trial.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates the Rule's core requirement that detention during investigation, inquiry, or trial cannot exceed the maximum imprisonment period for the offense, though it focuses specifically on the trial period rather than listing all three phases mentioned in the Rule.

results.parsed_rule: Before any person is released on bond or bail bond, a bond for such sum of money as the police officer or Court, as the case may be, thinks sufficient shall be executed by such person, and, when he is released on bond or bail bond, by one or more sufficient sureties conditioned that such person shall attend at the time and place mentioned in the bond, and shall continue so to attend until otherwise directed by the police officer or Court, as the case may be.
results.parsed_conclusion: Giving bail involves executing a bond rather than simply handing over cash, requiring both the accused and one or more sureties.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that a bond must be executed by the person being released and by one or more sureties (when released on bail bond), which directly supports the Conclusion's core claim that bail involves executing a bond with sureties rather than simply paying cash.

results.parsed_rule: An attested document not required by law to be attested may be proved as if it was unattested.
results.parsed_conclusion: The procedural benefit is that it allows over-formalized documents not required by law to be treated as unattested, streamlining the evidentiary process.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates that documents not legally required to be attested can be treated as unattested (which streamlines proof requirements), even though it adds interpretive language about "over-formalized documents" and "procedural benefit" that reasonably describes the practical effect of the Rule.

results.parsed_rule: Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a person has been trafficked, engages such person for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.parsed_conclusion: The man has committed the crime of Exploitation of a Trafficked Person as described in Section 144 of BNS 2023.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule directly establishes that engaging a trafficked person for sexual exploitation (knowingly or having reason to believe they were trafficked) constitutes a punishable crime, which aligns with the Conclusion's assertion that such conduct constitutes the crime of Exploitation of a Trafficked Person under Section 144 of BNS 2023.

results.parsed_rule: No particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required for the proof of any fact.
results.parsed_conclusion: The argument that the case must be dismissed due to lack of corroborating eyewitnesses will not succeed based on the statutory text provided.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove any fact, which directly contradicts the argument that a case must be dismissed for lacking a specific number (corroborating eyewitnesses), thus the Conclusion that such an argument will not succeed is supported by the Rule.

results.parsed_rule: "In every inquiry or trial, for the purpose of enabling the accused personally to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against him, the Court—(a) may at any stage, without previously warning the accused put such questions to him as the Court considers necessary; (b) shall, after the witnesses for the prosecution have been examined and before he is called on for his defence, question him generally on the case."
results.parsed_conclusion: Section 351 of BNSS 2023 mandates a mandatory mechanism for the accused to explain evidence through personal questioning by the court.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly requires the court to question the accused "for the purpose of enabling the accused personally to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against him," which directly supports the Conclusion's claim of a mandatory mechanism for personal questioning to explain evidence.

results.parsed_rule: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
results.parsed_conclusion: No, a six-year-old cannot be charged with manslaughter for accidentally shooting someone while holding a loaded gun, as such an act is not considered an offence by law.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that nothing done by a child under seven years of age is an offence, which directly supports the Conclusion that a six-year-old cannot be charged with manslaughter (or any offence).

results.parsed_rule: A report made by a police officer in a case which discloses, after investigation, the commission of a non-cognizable offense shall be deemed to be a complaint; and the police officer by whom such report is made shall be deemed to be the complainant.
results.parsed_conclusion: The case is legally categorized as a complaint based on the investigation's disclosure of a non-cognizable offense.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly states that a police report disclosing a non-cognizable offense after investigation "shall be deemed to be a complaint," which directly supports the Conclusion's claim that the case is legally categorized as a complaint based on such disclosure.

results.parsed_rule: "When any offence is committed in the presence of a Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, within his local jurisdiction, he may himself arrest or order any person to arrest the offender" (emphasis added) and "(2) Any Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, may at any time arrest or direct the arrest, in his presence, within his local jurisdiction, of any person for whose arrest he is competent at the time and in the circumstances to issue a warrant."
results.parsed_conclusion: A Magistrate must be present and have authority to issue a warrant for a past crime to arrest someone under these conditions.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule allows a Magistrate to arrest someone when an offence is committed in the Magistrate's presence (subsection 1), which does not require the crime to be "past" or pre-existing warrant authority, contradicting the Conclusion's characterization that both presence and prior warrant authority for a past crime are required.

results.parsed_rule: If a document is required by law to be attested, it shall not be used as evidence until one attesting witness at least has been called for the purpose of proving its execution, if there be an attesting witness alive, and subject to the process of the Court and capable of giving evidence.
results.parsed_conclusion: The lawyer must call at least one of the two witnesses to testify in order to comply with the law's requirement for proof of execution.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule requires that at least one attesting witness be called to prove execution when such a witness is alive, subject to the court's process, and capable of giving evidence, which directly supports the Conclusion's statement that the lawyer must call at least one witness to comply with the law's requirement for proof of execution.

results.parsed_rule: "A person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining within a period of thirty days from the date of framing of charge in the Court in which such offence is pending for trial."
results.parsed_conclusion: The court will not accept the man's application for plea bargaining as it has exceeded the statutory time limit of thirty days from the date of framing of charge.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule only establishes when an application *may* be filed (within thirty days), but does not state what happens if filed after that period or whether the court will or will not accept a late application.

results.parsed_rule: Whoever makes or counterfeits any seal, plate or other instrument for making an impression, intending that the same shall be used for the purpose of committing any forgery which would be punishable under section 338 of this Sanhita, or, with such intent, has in his possession any such seal, plate or other instrument, knowing the same to be counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.parsed_conclusion: Section 341 of BNS 2023 prescribes penalties for making or possessing counterfeit seals and plates with intent to commit forgery, as per the prescribed punishments.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates the Rule's core provisions regarding penalties for making or possessing counterfeit seals/plates with intent to commit forgery, even though it references "Section 341 of BNS 2023" (which is not mentioned in the Rule text itself but appears to be identifying where this Rule is codified) and summarizes rather than enumerates the specific punishments.

results.parsed_rule: "If, after taking the evidence for the prosecution, examining the accused and hearing the prosecution and the defence on the point, the Judge considers that there is no evidence that the accused committed the offence, the Judge shall record an order of acquittal."
results.parsed_conclusion: Three procedural steps must be completed after taking evidence for the prosecution and hearing both sides before a judge can consider recording an order of acquittal under Section 255.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule states that the judge records an order of acquittal *after* completing the three procedural steps (taking evidence, examining the accused, and hearing both sides), not that additional steps must be completed after those three steps as the Conclusion claims.

results.parsed_rule: Whoever abets the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force of the Government of India or attempts to seduce any such officer, soldier, sailor or airman from his allegiance or his duty, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.parsed_conclusion: The consequence for attempting to seduce military personnel from their duty is imprisonment for life or a term that may extend up to ten years, along with a fine.
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates the punishment specified in the Rule for attempting to seduce military personnel from their duty, correctly identifying both the imprisonment options (life or up to ten years) and the liability to fine.

results.parsed_rule: "(a) No Executive Magistrate or police officer acting under any of the said sections in good faith;"
results.parsed_conclusion: An Executive Magistrate or police officer acting in good faith is protected from being deemed to have committed an offence under sub-section (2).
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Conclusion accurately restates that Executive Magistrates and police officers acting in good faith receive protection (from being deemed to have committed an offence under sub-section (2)), which directly corresponds to what the Rule establishes through its "No..." formulation indicating an exemption or protection for such officials.

results.parsed_rule: (4) Where a superior officer of police has been appointed under section 177, the report shall, in any case in which the State Government by general or special order so directs, be submitted through that officer, and he may, pending the orders of the Magistrate, direct the officer in charge of the police station to make further investigation.
results.parsed_conclusion: The police cannot investigate the new evidence as the case has already been deemed closed upon filing their final report with the court.
results.explanation:
NOT_SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly allows a superior officer to direct further investigation even after a report has been submitted, directly contradicting the Conclusion's claim that police cannot investigate new evidence once a report is filed.

results.parsed_rule: For the purposes of section 85, “cruelty” means—(a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.
results.parsed_conclusion: Yes, this psychological abuse legally counts as "cruelty."
results.explanation:
SUPPORTED

The Rule explicitly defines cruelty to include wilful conduct likely to cause grave injury to the mental health of the woman, which encompasses psychological abuse.
